The incubation period of the Bronzed drongo (Dicrurus aeneus) has been documented under controlled conditions, with eggs maintained at 36 °C [T = 36 °C] hatching after approximately 13 days [ab = approximately 13 days]. This duration, measured in captive breeding studies, aligns with values reported for other small-bodied members of the Dicruridae family. The newly hatched nestlings emerge at a remarkably low mass, with the initial wet weight recorded at just 2.9 grams [Ww0 = 2.9 grams]. This neonatal mass is relatively modest compared to other passerines of similar adult size and likely reflects an altricial developmental strategy where rapid parental provisioning compensates for early energetic vulnerability. During the first week post-hatching, brooded chicks are entirely dependent on the parents for thermoregulation and food delivery, exhibiting steady gains in body mass as they consume a diet rich in arthropods captured in flight.

Fledging, defined as the achievement of sustained flight and the ability to leave the nest, occurs at 13 days after hatching [tx = 13 days after hatching] at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This relatively brief nestling phase is consistent with the life history of aerial insectivores that face high predation risk at the nest. Following nest departure, the fledglings remain dependent on parental care for several weeks, gradually refining their foraging skills. An important physiological benchmark is reached later: gonadal maturation, or the attainment of puberty, has been estimated to occur at 39 days since birth [tp = 39 days since birth] under this same thermal regime at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This interval between fledging and sexual maturity allows for substantial somatic development and the acquisition of foraging proficiency necessary for future reproductive success.

The ultimate adult body mass of the Bronzed drongo exhibits a distinct sexual dimorphism, as is common among many passerine birds. Adult females typically attain a final wet weight of 25.9 grams [Wwi = 25.9 grams], whereas adult males reach a slightly higher ultimate wet weight of 27 grams [Wwi = 27 grams]. This approximately four percent difference in mass is not a trivial morphological detail; it may reflect differential energetic demands associated with reproductive roles, with females perhaps investing more heavily in clutch formation while males allocate resources toward territorial defense and courtship displays. Both sexes achieve these asymptotic masses relatively quickly after fledging, a pattern typical of species with high post-fledging growth rates. The energetic cost of sustaining this adult body size under thermoneutral conditions has been directly measured through respirometry. The basal metabolic rate of adults, recorded under standard laboratory conditions, is 73.62 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 73.62 milliliters of oxygen per hour] at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This BMR value is elevated compared to some other Dicrurus species of equivalent mass, possibly reflecting the high activity levels associated with an aerial foraging lifestyle.

Reproductive output in the Bronzed drongo is relatively modest when considered on an annual basis. Field observations indicate that breeding pairs typically produce a clutch size of 2 to 4 eggs per nesting attempt [N_R_i = 2 to 4 eggs per nesting attempt], a figure consistent with many tropical insectivorous passerines that favor smaller broods but higher offspring quality. Furthermore, these same studies report that pairs usually manage one or two successful broods per year [F_R_i = one or two successful broods per year], depending on local food availability and seasonal rainfall patterns. In terms of life-history scheduling, the age at which individuals initiate their first breeding attempt has been recorded as approximately 438 days since birth [tR = approximately 438 days since birth] when maintained at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This delay of slightly over a year from hatching to first reproduction is characteristic of a slow-paced life-history strategy that allows significant investment in adult survival. The combination of moderate clutch sizes, limited annual broods, and deferred first reproduction suggests that the species faces strong selective pressure for adult persistence rather than maximizing immediate fecundity.

Longevity data for the Bronzed drongo, drawn from banding and recapture studies, indicate that the maximum lifespan in the wild is approximately 6.6 years [am = approximately 6.6 years], with individuals regularly surviving several breeding seasons under favorable environmental conditions at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This lifespan is substantial for a passerine of this body size and suggests a relatively low extrinsic mortality rate, perhaps linked to its agile flight and effective predator evasion tactics. The extended lifespan, when considered alongside the age at first reproduction of about 438 days, yields a lengthy reproductive window during which adults may produce multiple clutches each year. However, the finite annual reproductive capacity is constrained by the moderate clutch frequencies observed. The interplay between these life-history traits — a moderate adult body mass, a moderately elevated basal metabolic rate, deferred breeding, and a long lifespan — situates the Bronzed drongo as a species that prioritizes longevity and iteroparity, a strategy that may be particularly adaptive in the relatively stable, resource-predictable environments of tropical and subtropical forest canopies.
